name: envelope-letter
intent: Give clients a stable, value-like facade (the envelope) that owns and forwards every operation to an interchangeable implementation object (the letter), so the implementation type stays hidden behind one interface and can be replaced, reconfigured or swapped while the program runs.
problem: One interface must dispatch to several interchangeable implementations, but clients must not name them: the concrete type is chosen later (platform, configuration, plugin, test), and it may even change while the object lives. Hard-wiring the concrete class into the client re-couples the two, drags the implementation's header, module or library into every compile unit, and makes the choice global instead of per object.
context: Object-oriented code with a stable abstraction and several realizations - UI toolkits, protocol stacks, plugin hosts, numeric representations, test doubles - especially where the implementation type is a compile-time dependency that should not leak, where values must be copied, compared or stored in containers while still behaving polymorphically, or where the implementation is selected at run time rather than at construction.
benefits: Clients depend only on the envelope's interface: the letter's type, header/module and library stay out of the client's compile-time closure and can change without touching call sites.

Interchangeable realizations: different letters - or the same letter configured differently - are selected per object, per configuration or per test, and the letter can be exchanged at run time while the client keeps holding the same envelope.

Value-like usage on top of polymorphic behaviour: the envelope is copied, compared and stored by value while its letter stays a polymorphic object, which removes containers of raw pointers and the ownership bugs that come with them.
Implementation hiding and evolution: the letter's private members, helper headers and internal types never surface; the envelope's forwarding surface is the only published contract.
One place for cross-cutting concerns around the delegation: lazy creation, caching, logging, validation, reference counting or adaptation are added once in the envelope instead of in every call site.
tradeoffs: An extra indirection and usually a heap-allocated letter per envelope: every call pays a forwarding hop plus a virtual/table lookup, and the compiler can no longer inline or devirtualise the operation. The cost disappears for coarse operations and dominates for tiny ones.

Copy semantics must be decided explicitly: a value envelope needs a deep clone, while a shallow copy silently shares one mutable letter between copies and surfaces as aliasing bugs far away from the copy site.

Forwarding is boilerplate: every operation of the letter interface has to be repeated on the envelope (or generated by a language facility), and the interface cannot be extended without changing both types.

The hidden implementation cannot be reached from the visible type: letters that need context from the envelope must be handed an explicit back-reference (the handle/body invocation-context problem), and refinements of hidden letter subtypes cannot be invoked through an envelope subclass.

Failure modes move rather than disappear: the letter is often created at a different time than the envelope (lazy creation, plugin load, deserialisation), so empty, dangling and half-initialised states must be designed instead of relying on the constructor.
Debugging and profiling get harder: stack frames jump from the envelope into an invisible implementation, and type-based tooling shows only the envelope while the behaviour lives in the letter.

participants.responsibility: The stable, value-like class clients use; it owns or references the letter and forwards every operation of the letter interface to it. It holds no domain state of its own beyond the letter reference and whatever representation policy (ownership, cloning, caching) it enforces.
The abstraction the envelope dispatches through. It declares exactly the operations the envelope forwards - the smaller it is, the cheaper the forwarding and the less implementation detail leaks.
A concrete realization that holds the real state and behaviour. Several letters implement the same interface and are interchangeable behind the envelope; the client never names them.
Creates, clones or resolves letters (by prototype, configuration, platform or service id) so neither the envelope nor its clients mention a concrete letter type.
Uses envelopes as ordinary values: constructs, copies, compares and stores them and calls operations on them without knowing which letter is in place.

use_cases: UI and graphics toolkits where shapes, widgets or documents are handed around by value while drawing, layout and event handling live in replaceable backend objects (Coplien's widget-library example; the hush class library used exactly this handle/body split).

Numeric and domain value types whose arithmetic depends on the representation (real, complex, rational, interval, money with different rounding rules): the envelope is the number the program uses, the letter implements the operations for one representation.

Library APIs that must not expose the implementation type in a public header or module: the envelope declares the API, the letter is only visible in the source file — the compile-firewall use of the same mechanics.
Test seams: production code keeps using one envelope type while per-test fakes, spies or recorded letters are substituted, including for behaviour that is otherwise slow, remote or non-deterministic.

Plugin and driver dispatch: a loaded module supplies the letter, the host keeps only the envelope facade and the stable interface; swapping the loaded module swaps the letter for new objects (and, if the envelope allows it, for existing ones).
Adapting a legacy subsystem behind a modern interface: the envelope carries the new API and an adapter letter forwards into the old implementation, so callers migrate without the old code changing.
COM/OLE Automation and similar component frameworks: the public COM interface is an envelope, the hidden implementation object is the letter; IUnknown itself is a form of handle/body.

ORM and data-mapper proxies: an envelope represents an entity, a letter implements the persistence logic; the envelope can be passed around by value while the persistence backend is swapped between a test double and a live database connection.
Copy-on-write data structures: std::string and Qt's implicitly-shared classes use a handle/body split internally to defer the copy of large payloads until a mutation occurs.
Cross-language bridging (Python/C++, Java JNI, Node.js native addons): the native implementation is the letter, the language-bound wrapper is the envelope that hides the FFI boundary.

Java AWT widgets: java.awt.Component is the envelope the program manipulates, and each heavyweight component forwards painting, resizing and input to a native peer object behind the java.awt.peer.ComponentPeer interface — the letter is supplied by the platform toolkit, and the JDK deprecated direct peer manipulation (getPeer()) precisely so clients see only the envelope.

JDBC: Connection, Statement and ResultSet are the stable envelope the application compiles against, while each vendor driver supplies interchangeable letters implementing the same interfaces — application code never names a driver class and swaps databases by swapping the driver at deployment time.

Java NIO.2 filesystems: Path and Files act as envelopes whose operations dispatch to a provider-specific letter chosen per FileSystem through FileSystemProvider, so the same API drives both on-disk files and entries in a mounted ZIP filesystem.
avoid_when: Only one implementation exists and no seam, swap or copy semantics is needed - a plain class or a free function is simpler and the indirection buys nothing.

The set of realizations is closed and known at compile time: a sealed hierarchy with exhaustive matching, a tagged union or std::variant documents the cases and keeps the compiler's exhaustiveness check.
Only dependency inversion is wanted (one implementation chosen once and injected): dependency injection, a factory call or Strategy at the construction site already covers it without a second type.

The language dispatches through interfaces natively and reference semantics are acceptable (Go, Java, C#, Python, TypeScript): an interface-typed field is the idiomatic form and a copying envelope wrapper adds a type for nothing.
Hot inner loops over trivially small values where the forwarding hop and the heap-allocated letter cost more than the operation itself.
anti_patterns: Envelope that hands out its letter (public field, getter returning the implementation, raw pointer accessor): clients downcast again and the decoupling is gone.
Copy-constructing an envelope whose letter is shared and mutable, so two 'values' silently alias each other's state.
God-envelope that re-exports an entire subsystem's API instead of one narrow abstraction: the forwarding surface grows with the implementation, so every implementation change reaches the envelope.
Rebuilding the pattern by hand in a language that already delegates (Kotlin's `by`, Ruby's Forwardable, Scala 3's export): stubs written where the compiler or stdlib would generate them.
Wrapping a single concrete class behind an interface 'for future flexibility', adding a hop and a second type for a variation that never arrives.
design_principles: Separation of interface and implementation (information hiding): the envelope is the published interface, the letter is the hidden decision that may change.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: the envelope's field is typed by the letter interface and the concrete letter is only named in a factory.
Composition over inheritance: the envelope delegates to the letter instead of inheriting behaviour, so the implementation can change without changing the client's type.
Single responsibility: the envelope manages representation and forwarding, the letter implements behaviour - neither should do the other's job.
Liskov substitutability: every letter must honour the letter interface's contract, because the client can no longer see which letter it is holding.
best_practices: Decide and document the copy policy before writing the envelope: deep clone for value semantics, or an explicitly shared immutable letter for handle semantics. A shallow copy of a shared mutable letter is the pattern's classic aliasing bug.

Keep the letter interface as small as the abstraction allows; forwarding cost, clone cost and the leakage of implementation detail all scale with its size. Every extra operation on the interface is another forwarding stub to maintain.

Use the language's delegation facility where it exists — operator-> overloading in C++, `by` in Kotlin, Forwardable/DelegateClass in Ruby, export in Scala 3, Deref in Rust — instead of hand-written stub methods.

Never expose the letter through the envelope's public API (no public getter, raw pointer or field accessor). If a caller genuinely needs the implementation, hand it a narrow adapter interface; downcasting re-couples clients and defeats the decoupling.
Create letters through a factory, prototype registry or builder so neither the envelope nor its clients ever name a concrete letter type.
Model the absent-letter state explicitly: an empty/optional letter is better than a null pointer that forces every call site to null-check.

If the letter needs context from its envelope (a q-pointer in the d-pointer idiom), pass a weak reference or a dedicated context object — never a raw pointer that outlives the envelope. More critically, a Private destructor must NEVER call back into the public class: some std::unique_ptr implementations dereference a nullptr before invoking the destructor, producing undefined behaviour.
Measure before wrapping a hot path: the forwarding hop and virtual-table lookup add a constant cost that is negligible for coarse operations and measurable for tiny ones (e.g. a scalar getter).

For thread-safe shared letters, use a shared-ownership smart pointer (std::shared_ptr) and consider whether the letter's state needs its own locking; copying the envelope must not race with mutation of the shared letter.
When the envelope must satisfy a standard-library container or range interface, forward those constraints explicitly and ensure the letter implementation honours them.
Preserve const-correctness on the envelope: const-envelope reads must not mutate the letter. If the letter uses copy-on-write, detach on any non-const operation.
sources: Coplien, Advanced C++ Programming Styles and Idioms (Addison-Wesley, 1992), Chapters on Handle/Body, Envelope/Letter (pp. 179–184) and Virtual Constructor — the canonical origin of the idiom.
Linda Rising (ed.), Patterns Almanac (Addison-Wesley, 1999), entries for Handle/Body (pp. 179–182) and Envelope/Letter (pp. 182–184) — clear summaries of Coplien's multi-page treatment.

Griffiths, 'Separating Interface and Implementation in C++', ACCU Overload Journal, Issue 66, 2004 — compares Cheshire Cat, Envelope/Letter, Interface Class and Non-Virtual Public Interface with performance analysis; notes Envelope/Letter is the slowest due to two virtual-dispatch hops but that the overhead is rarely significant.

Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2003), Envelope Wrapper [online] https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/EnvelopeWrapper.html — same concept applied in messaging/integration architectures.

Qt Wiki, D-Pointer [online] https://wiki.qt.io/D-Pointer — canonical real-world OSS usage of the handle/body split with copy-on-write semantics and q-ptr back-reference pattern; every Qt public class uses it.

Barker, 'The Envelope Pattern of Content Management' [online] https://deanebarker.net/tech/blog/envelope-pattern-of-content-management/ — practical CMS/data-hub application of the envelope separating instance data from metadata/headers.

POSA1, Buschmann et al., Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture: A System of Patterns (Wiley, 1996) — documents Handle/Body as a C++ idiom pattern; Envelope-Letter is the run-time-polymorphic specialisation of it.

Coplien, 'Advanced C++ Idioms' idiom sheet [online] https://www.laputan.org/pub/sag/coplien-idioms.pdf — canonical statement of Envelope/Letter and Handle/Body: the handle provides the common virtual interface, every letter derives from a common body base, and the handle forwards so the body can be replaced at run time ('metamorphosis') without changing the published API.

Pearce, 'Handle/Body (Envelope-Letter)' [online] http://www.cs.sjsu.edu/faculty/pearce/patterns/hanbod/hanbod.html — course reproduction of Coplien's Number envelope with Rational/Complex/Real/Integer letters, including the orthodox-canonical-form obligations the handle must honour.

Oracle, java.awt.Component javadoc [online] https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.desktop/java/awt/Component.html — official documentation of AWT's envelope/letter split: heavyweight components delegate to native toolkit peers, programs must not manipulate peers directly, and Swing components dropped the peer entirely.

Software Patterns Lexicon, 'Bridge Pattern for Java Abstraction Boundaries' [online] https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/java/structural-patterns/bridge-pattern/ — real-world mappings of the envelope/letter mechanics in the JDK: JDBC drivers behind Connection/Statement, AWT ComponentPeer, NIO.2 Path providers, and SLF4J-style logging bridges.

'Is the PIMPL idiom really used in practice?' [online] https://stackoverflow.com/questions/8972588/is-the-pimpl-idiom-really-used-in-practice — practitioner criticism: indirection cost, extra allocation, memory and debugging overhead; consensus is to apply the handle/body split selectively at API boundaries, not universally.

Bankov, 'Don't Use unique_ptr for PIMPL' [online] https://ibob.bg/blog/2019-11-07/dont-use-unique_ptr-for-pimpl/ — lifetime and value-semantics traps when the letter is held in std::unique_ptr, including libc++ null-dereference crashes during destruction.
